body_markdown:
*TL;DR: Slipstream agents do the engineering work at Glide on their own. They very frequently would stop to ask a person something that the team had already decided. In the worst case they'd act on an answer that was out of date. The constraint on their autonomy was context. We built a shared memory that we call the brain and made it fast and cheap enough to use for every message. For any questions that required the team to make a decision, agents with the brain got it right in 10 of 13 cases. The ones without the brain got it right in 1 of 11 cases. A memory answer now takes around 10 seconds and costs a third of a cent. This post goes through each of the steps and the numbers.*


## Why Context Was the Bottleneck


Our earlier Slipstream articles looked at how the agents at Glide ship and maintain software. At this stage our agents are running 20 workflows with no one looking at each run.


They could get to every major platform we use on a day to day basis. They had no context at all of the kind of thing a teammate would have. No implicit knowledge. What we'd decided last week, who owned a particular feature and which plan had been reversed. An agent looking at our AI spend asked the team a question we'd already answered.


Every question an agent passed on to a person was work that the agent hadn't actually completed itself. The more questions we were passing on to the team the further we were from true autonomy. The lack of context was the root of the problem and that was the bottleneck.


We spent the last 6 weeks working on this. Here's the full journey we went through to get to where we are, including what didn't work.


## When Agents Have Tools, But No Context


Our engineering agent had MCP connections to GitHub, Slack and our monitoring tools. If you asked it "why did we close that incident?" or "who owns onboarding?" it would go and search those systems live, read the results and write you an answer.


We wrote 50 questions on our own engineering work and asked each one three times. An answer counted when it was right and named its source.


Agent with MCP tools only


Right, with a source 29%


Cost per answer $0.49


Median time to answer 52 seconds


Out-of-date answers 32 of 123


The worst bit was the out of date answers. They'd find an old Slack thread, they'd completely miss the later decision that had superseded it and then they'd report that as the current position with absolute confidence.


## Building a Shared Memory for the Team


The brain is a collection of some 4000 short facts, each with a date and a source. It's constructed in four stages and the stages keep going.


**Collect.** Scheduled jobs check our public Slack channels, GitHub, and meeting summaries all day. We leave out private channels and direct messages to uphold privacy and to keep the shared memory focused on company-wide decisions, rather than private or sensitive conversations. The jobs skip messages written by agents and bots, so the brain only learns from people.


**Distill.** An agent goes through each batch of events and writes down a fact only if it passes a certain test: would an agent somewhere else be asking the wrong question or making the wrong decision without it? Most events fail that test. So far 13,965 events have yielded 4,148 facts. Each fact has a record of where it came from, the date, a link back to the source and whether it was said in a conversation or in a PR.


**Reconcile.** People will often change their minds. Before it writes a new fact the agent will look at the earlier facts on that same subject. If the new fact supersedes the old one then the old one is marked as replaced and retained.


**Build the map.** Each night a job takes the facts and attaches them to named things (e.g. features, decisions). A person made a decision and that decision was the state of a feature. That's what the ontology is.


We did October in one pass and then switched the daily jobs on. 4,942 events became 1,580 facts for $29 which is less than two cents a fact.


### Who Owns What


People and business areas come from our team directory. The brain works out which area owns a feature based on who made the decision about it. A question such as 'who owns onboarding?' would then end up on the record that has the current state, the owner and the history. The diagram above is an example of such a record.


### Where the Brain Lives


We store the brain as plain markdown files in a git repo and host it on Cloudflare Artifacts. One file per day, one fact per line (who said it, source and date).


An agent discovers a fact by searching the text and reading the file. A replaced fact remains in the file with a marker indicating what has replaced it. Every change is a commit so that we can read the brain's own history.


### Dreaming


Agents also maintain their own notes in the same type of repository. There is one shared index file which is read by every agent on every turn. Notes written during a task will simply repeat themselves and become stale. A memory agent therefore runs once a night to clean them up. Also known as dreaming.


In one pass, the memory agent:


- corrects a note contradicted by a newer fact in the brain
- merges notes that say the same thing
- removes notes that are no longer true
- moves detail out of an index file that has grown too long
- shares a note that two or more agents need
- checks about five notes against their sources and marks them as checked


Every change it makes references its evidence and is a single commit. A pass can change at most 25 files in one memory file, anything beyond that goes into its report for a human to read. The brain's own facts are not available to it at all, they are the evidence it uses to correct everything else. On the first night it tidied the index files the index for one workflow went from 161% of its size limit down to 24%.


The agent looks in the brain first and only goes to live systems for live data.


MCP tools only With the brain


Right, with a source 29% 71%


Cost per answer $0.49 $0.16


Median time to answer 52 seconds 23 seconds


Out-of-date answers 32 of 123 2 of 123


That was a massive improvement and it immediately raised a very clear next issue. All of those answers were generated by Claude Opus 5.5 (the most powerful and most expensive model we have). A lookup in a memory file should be both common and cheap.


## Making Memory Fast and Accessible


We ran the same 41 questions against seven models. Five of them completed the full comparison.


Haiku 5.5 was the one that stood out. It was two answers behind Opus at around one fortieth of the cost.


## Raising the Bar on Accuracy


Two things about our test actually put us off before we'd accepted that result.


Firstly a Claude model was grading the answers and it was winning hands down. We then added in a Gemini and a GPT judge and only counted an answer as correct if two of the three judges agreed. The judges were all very different in terms of how strict they were.


Second, 41 questions were too few. The same setup could swing ten points between two runs. When we read the misses one by one, we also found errors in our own answer key. The list of expected answers, known as the answer key, scores each reply. We expected a few outdated answers. Some were so long that the grader penalized a correct short answer.


We've written a fresh set of 121 questions. Each expected answer has been checked against the brain by three independent reviewers, plus human review. That was all done prior to the set going in. Each setup gives you 363 graded answers (363 answers in total, as each question is asked 3 times).


We wanted Haiku at 90%+ before using it on any real questions.


## Unlocking the Team's Full History


We've read all of Haiku's wrong answers and most of them fell into two categories.


In the first group Haiku never spotted the fact that was the key to the answer. The root of the problem was our own search tool. When a newer fact replaced an older one the search tool simply omitted the older one. That's fine for "what is true now". It fails for "what changed" and "what was true on October 20" as those answers reside in the facts which have been replaced.


552 of our 4,019 facts were hidden in this manner.


We found Opus had been working around the gap by opening up whole day files. Ten or eleven reads per question. Haiku stopped earlier and just gave us what it had.


We added a search option which includes history. Haiku hit 93.9% with no other changes and the fix is good for every model that uses the brain.


## The Power of Plain English


In the second group Haiku found the correct fact and then undermined its own answer. It wrote 'probably' or added 'I could not confirm this shipped' to a fact which did in fact record the ship.


We tried the cheap fix before building anything. We gave Haiku six rules in plain English:


- Open with the direct answer.
- Treat a recorded change as done.
- When a fact points to another fact, follow the pointer.
- Treat the same label as the same thing.
- Answer a question about a past date as fact, using the value from that date.
- Search history for any question on history.


Haiku got to 96.4%. Cost and speed remained unchanged.


Haiku 5.5 on 363 answers Right


Straight swap from Opus 89.3%


After the search fix 93.9%


With the six rules 96.4%


Opus 5.5, for reference 95.9%


## Working Smarter: Routing the Work


A fast model for brain questions only really helps if the agent knows which of the messages it's receiving are actually being answered via the brain. Most of what our agents get is work of some sort (e.g. make a code change, review a PR etc) and that's where you need the full model and all of its tools.


So we have a tiny decision model in front of every message asking one question: can the brain on its own answer that?


The design is very one-sided. A brain question that the sorter sends to the strong model will cost more, but will still get a correct answer. A coding question sent to the small model would be a genuine failure. Anything the sorter is in any doubt about will remain on the strong model.


In the test the sorter sent 104 of the 112 brain questions to Haiku. It held all of the other 63 messages (the lot of coding stuff and the mixed requests) on the strong model.


## What Didn't Work (And Why)


Four ideas looked good in our assessment but didn't perform in the benchmarks.


**Sorted by difficulty.** Our first sorter sent the easy questions to Haiku and the history questions to Opus. Accuracy held and cost fell by as much as 50%. Speed didn't really change as the hard questions still took Opus 19 seconds to answer which set the average.


**A lookup helper.** We had Opus hand its memory lookups over to Haiku and do the rest of the work. That saved 2 cents per answer at the expense of 3 seconds as Opus then had to do its own searches to verify the result. The feature is built and currently switched off.


**More thinking time.** Giving Haiku a larger reasoning budget made it slower and it gained less than the six rules did.


**Vector search.** We did semantic search over the same facts for the first question set and got 67% correct as opposed to 71% for the files using the map.


## The Results: Better, Faster, Cheaper


“


Massive change in the Slack interaction experience when you feel it's faster than even chatting with a colleague”


Tristan L'Abbé


VP of Design


## Lessons for Building Autonomous Agents


Context limited autonomy before the model did. Our agents had the access and the skill. They lacked the tacit knowledge that every team in the organization has.


The model was actually the last thing that needed to change. The biggest gains were actually earlier on in the process: just getting the facts down in the first place. A huge improvement in performance came from structuring the facts in a flat file format which the models can then easily query.


Once those were sorted the smallest model in the range actually beat the biggest one on this task. We're now running memory questions on the cheaper, faster model for every agent at Glide. The "strong" model is doing the work it was built for. The agents have significantly more efficacy, much higher accuracy and lower cost. 96% correct vs 29% at the start, at $0.003 per answer vs $0.49.


[Simon Fletcher](https://www.glideapps.com/blog/author/simon-fletcher)


Principal Software Engineer at Glide
